newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore talks fundraising and human rights in China.
newsitem.headline: Gore talks fundraising and human rights in China.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore on Wednesday ended two days of talks with Chinese leaders, saying allegations that Beijing tried to illegally fund the U.S. Democratic Party should not disrupt Sino-U.S. relations.
Gore said he had raised such touchy topics as human rights and trade with his Chinese hosts, but added the talks had been friendly and that prospects for improved ties were bright.
A probe into reports China tried to make donations to U.S. politicians should not affect Sino-U.S. relations, he said, but it would be a serious matter if such charges were proved.
Gore said his visit would help pave the way for an exchange of state visits, with Chinese President Jiang Zemin scheduled to travel to Washington in the autumn.
"Our discussions were productive, friendly, searching and above all wide-ranging," Gore told a news briefing after meeting Jiang.
The vice president, the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit China since Beijing crushed pro-democracy protests in Tiananmen Square in 1989, met Chinese Premier Li Peng on Tuesday.

"Our vision is that the U.S. and China, as friends and partners, will share a prosperous and peaceful future of free minds and free markets," Gore told a gathering of students at the capital's elite Qinghua University.
He told reporters that he had raised specific human rights cases in meetings with the Chinese leaders and that his statements had met with a better response than in the past.
But he declined to say if he had won any concessions from Beijing on improving its human rights record -- long a source of bitter contention in the Sino-U.S. relationship.

"As to why I thought they were more receptive, it has to do with the language that was used, the muted tone of the response compared to previous conversations I've had with these leaders on this topic," Gore said.
Gore said Premier Li had strongly denied reports that China tried to illegally funnel cash into U.S. Democratic Party campaign coffers during last year's U.S. elections.
"The discussions of the (payments) controversy now, pending the completion of the investigation, should not affect the relationship between China and the United States," he said.
"I... said that the U.S. views these allegations as very serious, however, they're the subject of an ongoing criminal investigation in our Justice Department," he said.

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) had warned six members of Congress last year they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign funds from foreign corporations.
"Should the allegations prove to be true, then of course that would be a different matter and I made it clear that that would be serious indeed," Gore said.

The uproar over possible campaign contributions is particularly awkward for Gore because part of the FBI probe involves determining whether or not China tried to secretly fund President Bill Clinton and his campaign.

The fundraising issue partly overshadowed the goals of a mission that Gore had hoped would highlight his diplomatic skills and help position him to contest the presidency in 2000, but the vice president said his talks had been successful.
"I think we have done some good work here on behalf of the United States and on behalf of the relationship between the United States and China and I think this kind of work has to continue," he said.
The U.S. vice president said he had pulled no punches in talks on trade, telling Chinese leaders they needed to do more to open their markets to American goods.
"I expressed the need of greater access to China's market for American goods and services," he said.
Both sides had affirmed that Jiang would visit the United States in autumn, and officials were working on setting dates, he said. Clinton is expected to visit China in 1998.

Gore said Washington expected China to live up to its promises on Hong Kong after the British colony returned to Beijing rule on July 1 -- another issue that has caused Sino-U.S. friction in recent weeks.
"We expect China to honour its commitments," he said.
